# CI configuration data

## `build-matrix.json`

JSON array of objects `{ "host", "distro", "container" }` passed to `build-sign-deploy.yaml` as `strategy.matrix.include` (via `fromJson`).

**Removing** a distro, changing a runner label, or bumping a container image pin needs only this file. Hotfix branches can merge or cherry-pick such changes without touching workflow logic.

**Adding** a new distro unconditionally requires `.github/bin/install_deps.bash` (add an `install_deps_<distro>` function and a `case` arm; the build fails with `Unsupported distro` otherwise). Depending on the distro's package family and toolchain, it may also require:
- `.github/bin/build_edition.bash` — only if the distro needs a new toolchain arm (e.g. a new EL gcc-toolset version; same-family distros like a new Ubuntu release are covered by the existing `ubuntu*|debian*` glob).
- `.github/workflows/build-sign-deploy.yaml` — only if the distro needs new prereqs or build-time workarounds not covered by the existing glob patterns in the `Install prereqs` step.

Invalid JSON fails fast in the `setup` job, which runs `jq empty` on this file before the build matrix fans out (not later at the downstream `fromJson`). Still, use your editor or any JSON checker before pushing if you want an even earlier signal.

## C client versions (`build-and-test.yaml`)

The C client refs the server is tested against are matrix data too, but they live inline in `.github/workflows/build-and-test.yaml` as `jobs.client-test.strategy.matrix.client` rather than in a file here. The reason `build-matrix.json` is separate — hotfix branches cherry-picking distro changes without touching workflow logic — barely applies here: `build-and-test.yaml` runs automatically only on PRs to `master`. It *can* be dispatched manually against any branch, hotfix branches included, but a dispatched run narrows the list with the `client_versions` input, so a hotfix branch never needs to cherry-pick a change to the default.

**Bumping the list** is a manual step on each C client minor release: add the new tag, drop whichever old one no longer needs cover. The literal in `strategy.matrix.client` is the only copy — the `workflow_dispatch` input deliberately has no `default:`, so an empty input falls through to that same literal. Nothing enforces the bump, so a stale list quietly keeps burning CI on versions that stopped mattering.

**What an entry costs.** One `client-test` job per distro per PR. It does *not* cost a server build: `build` runs once per distro and `client-test` installs its package artifact, so adding a client version no longer multiplies `Build and package` (~13 min) or `Run unit tests` (~3.6 min). It does cost each leg's own setup — the client dep install (~25 s), the enterprise clone for `features.conf` (~4 s), the package download and install, and the server cold start — which is why a leg runs ~3 min rather than ~2 min of client work.

**Mutable vs immutable refs.** Tags (`7.4.0`, `7.5.0`) are reproducible; `stage` is a branch, so re-running an unchanged server commit can check out a different client tree and get a different result. `stage` is labelled a pre-release ref by `report_client_test.bash`, which classifies by the shape of the ref string (`N.N.N` or `vN.N.N` → shipped client, anything else → pre-release) rather than by a matrix flag. A branch-valued entry therefore needs no flag, and must **not** be given an `include:` row of its own: a row keyed on a specific `client` value spawns a phantom matrix combination — with no `distro`, no `os` and no `container` — whenever `workflow_dispatch` narrows the list so that value is absent.

**A dispatched ref is checked before it is checked out.** `client_versions` cannot introduce a new ref *into the checkout*; it can and does introduce one into the matrix, because `fromJSON` consumes the input verbatim. A guard step immediately before the C client checkout rejects anything that is not `N.N.N`, `vN.N.N` or `stage`, and being placed there its implicit `success()` gates the checkout too, so a rejected ref never reaches third-party code. The cost of that placement is that the leg has already spawned, installed the package and cold-started `asd` by the time the ref is refused — twelfth step of seventeen. Validating the array ahead of the matrix, in a `setup` job that emits it as an output, is what would make the narrowing claim true rather than merely enforced. Without it, `actions/checkout` resolves any ref the remote advertises — `aerospike-client-c` is public, so `refs/pull/N/head` names a branch belonging to any account that has ever opened a PR against it. The dispatcher can already run code in this job, so that is not an escalation for them; it is a confused-deputy step, where "dispatch `build-and-test` with `["refs/pull/412/head"]` so we can check my client fix against your server" reads as an ordinary request. Widen the pattern deliberately if `stage`-like branches multiply — the point is that the set lives in the repository.

Do **not** derive this list from the client's released tags at run time. A new upstream tag would silently change what CI covers with no commit here — exactly the non-reproducibility the pinning exists to remove.

**Reading the result at a glance.** Three surfaces carry it, at three resolutions.

The **jobs list and the run status** are binary: any failing test case fails that leg's `client-test` job, so the run goes red. A job conclusion has no third colour to spend, which is the whole reason the other two surfaces exist.

The **check run** per leg, `C client <ref> (<distro>)`, grades it: green for a clean run, red for any failed test case, grey (`neutral`) when the tests never ran — the client did not build, an earlier gating step failed, or the `build` job did not produce this distro's package. The count is of individual test cases, summed from the client's `<suite>: N/M tests passed.` lines and cross-checked against its run total, and it is in the check run's own title — so one broken suite does not read the same as a wholesale break even though both are red. **Five** states take red regardless of the count, because in each of them the count does not mean what it says:

- `asd` was gone before the tests finished — checked by process *state*, not by `kill -0`, which succeeds on a zombie and would make this arm unreachable on the three `el9` legs (a job container's PID 1 is `tail -f /dev/null`, which never reaps).
- the test step was killed mid-run, detected by a sentinel the killed step cannot write.
- **no `<suite>: N/M` line parsed at all.** Not conditioned on the run total also being absent: with the total present and parsing, the count is zero and the leg would otherwise grade green under the words "all 0 suites passed", so a drift in the per-suite format alone would turn every leg permanently and silently green.
- **suite lines parsed, but the run never reached its total line** — a crashed test binary, an OOM kill, or `make -k`. `make` *returns* in these, so the sentinel cannot see them; the missing total is the only signal that the count is a lower bound.
- `make test` failed while every suite it reported passed.

Re-running a leg updates its existing check run rather than adding a second one with a different conclusion.

**There is no amber check-run conclusion, and that is deliberate.** An earlier revision published `action_required` for 1–4 failures. Measured against this PR's own check runs, that is not a third colour anywhere a reader actually looks: `gh pr checks` prints it as `fail`, the commit's `statusCheckRollup` is `FAILURE`, and the payload carries no `actions[]` — which is the thing GitHub pairs that conclusion with. It would also block a merge exactly as `failure` does the moment these checks are made required, silently and with no code change here. So the 1–4 tier lives in the count in the title, and in the job summary's alert colour, which does render.

The `asd.log` / `client-tests.log` artifact is uploaded on any leg the **reporter** graded as anything but a pass — the step is ordered after it and gated on `steps.report.outputs.conclusion`, the grade the reporter publishes. Two weaker predicates were tried first, and each was blind to a region. The test step's own outcome misses three of the five states above, which leave it green — so the upload was skipped on exactly the legs whose check-run body says to go read `asd.log`. The reporter's *exit status* misses the opposite region: it collapses `success` and `neutral` onto 0 by design, so every leg that failed before the client build exits 0 while grading grey — a package that would not download, a failed install, a rejected ref, and above all an `asd` that died during cold start, which is the one case `asd.log` exists for. Only the published grade separates all five.

All of that grading lives in `.github/bin/report_client_test.bash` rather than in a `run:` block, so `shfmt` and the pre-commit `shellcheck` hook reach it — both target shell *files* — and so `.github/bin/test_report_client_test.bash` can drive every branch from fixture logs with `curl` stubbed. That suite runs as `runner / client test report tests`; add a case to it before changing the grading rules. Six of its cases are gated on host capabilities (`/proc`, `readlink -f /proc/<pid>/exe` answering, TCP 3000 free), which a developer machine may genuinely lack; in CI an unmet gate is a hard failure rather than a skip, and the suite asserts its own case count, so a green run means a known set of cases ran and not an unknown subset. It also asserts the parts of `build-and-test.yaml` the reporter depends on the workflow to uphold — the bare-name contract, the artifact upload gating on the published grade, the reporter step not being `continue-on-error`, and the check run hanging off the PR head — because reverting any of those used to cost nothing.

The **job summary** repeats that grade as a coloured GFM alert (`TIP`/`WARNING`/`CAUTION`/`NOTE`) naming the failing suites, and it is the one surface with a real third colour: `WARNING` is the 1–4 tier, `CAUTION` 5 or more. That is the only place the alert and the check-run conclusion disagree, and the only place either of them can. Alerts are the only colour available there — the markdown sanitizer strips `style` attributes, so `<span style="color:…">` renders as text.

None of this blocks a merge: master has no required status checks, in branch protection or in either ruleset. Red means *a reader should look*, not *you cannot merge*. Marking these checks required is what would change that, and it would promote every one of the client's own flaky tests into a merge gate — see the C client bugs behind the failures these legs report today.

**A client build failure is deliberately not a job failure.** A client that will not compile in our CI image says nothing about this server, so it reports grey and lets the job pass. Only a test *disagreement* is red.

**The enterprise feature key is reachable from the client build, and that is not fixable here.** `client-test` exports `FEATUREKEY` inside the `Start Aerospike server` step rather than writing it to `$GITHUB_ENV`, and deletes the enterprise checkout before the C client is checked out. Both narrow the surface and neither closes it: `gh-action.conf` reads the key as `feature-key-file env-b64:FEATUREKEY`, so `asd` holds the blob in its own environment for its whole lifetime — which spans the client build and tests by design, because the tests need a live server. `asd` runs under the same uid as the client's `make` (no `user`/`group` stanza, so no privilege drop; root throughout on `el9`) and its pid is in the workspace, so `/proc/<pid>/environ` is a one-line read for anything running during `make`.

What *is* done here is `::add-mask::`, and it is narrower than it looks. The masker runs on the runner's log-write path, so it redacts the job log and nothing else; it has no hook into file writes. `client-tests.log` comes from `make test 2>&1 | tee`, which writes raw bytes to the file and only forwards a copy through the runner, and `asd.log` and `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` are files too — so the uploaded artifact, readable for 7 days by anyone with read access to this repo, carries the value unmasked. **The artifact route is open, not closed**, and it shares a root cause with the `/proc` route. Closing either needs a dedicated, short-dated CI-only feature key for `gh-action.conf` (the cheap answer, and a provisioning decision rather than a workflow one) or a separate service uid, which does nothing for the `el9` legs where everything is root. Dropping `client-tests.log` from the artifact would close the artifact route on its own, at the cost of the 7-day retention of test output for a leg whose job log has aged out.

**The reporter runs in the same job as third-party code, and holds `checks: write`.** `report_client_test.bash` lives in the workspace, one directory over from where the client's `make` ran as the same uid, and its inputs (`client-tests.log`, `asd.pid`, `client-tests-finished`) are in that workspace too — so code execution during `make` in `aerospike-client-c` at the ref under test can overwrite either the reporter or what it grades, and the reporter's exit status *is* the leg's conclusion. The token is piped to `curl` as a config on stdin (`-K -`) rather than passed in argv. That narrows one reader — `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` is mode 0444, so any uid on the box can scrape it while a call is in flight — and it closes nothing: `CHECKS_TOKEN` is a step-level `env:` entry, so it sits in `/proc/<pid>/environ` of the reporter and of every `curl` it spawns, mode 0400 but readable by the same uid the client's `make` ran under, for the whole step. That is the same no-write read over a *longer* window, and it is the deferred split, not the config, that closes it. Stdin rather than a file in `RUNNER_TEMP` for the same class of reason: a config file advertises its own path in argv, outlives the call, and — planted before the reporter runs — would be honoured verbatim, and `-K` sets any curl option and not just a header, so a planted config can redirect both calls and turn a published check run into a silent `::warning::`. A third channel needs neither the `/proc` read nor a workspace write: every `run:` step is handed `$GITHUB_PATH`, and a line the client's own `make` appends to that file is prepended to `PATH` for every *later* step of the job — including the reporter, whose interpreter and every tool it calls (`curl`, `sed`, `tr`, `cat`, `readlink`, and the `command -v curl` probe) are unqualified. A planted `curl` is handed the config on stdin and holds `CHECKS_TOKEN` in its own environ regardless, so the argv-versus-stdin distinction is moot against it; `$GITHUB_ENV` and `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` are the same file-command mechanism. Pointing the two client steps at scratch `GITHUB_PATH`/`GITHUB_ENV` files closes one spelling of five — overwriting `report_client_test.bash` itself needs no `PATH` at all — and doing it with a `${{ runner.temp }}` path would re-enter the host-versus-container bug the bare-name contract exists to prevent, so it is enumerated here rather than patched. None of that is containment. The fix is to split the reporter into a `needs: client-test` job that checks out no third-party code — the leg grades with no token and uploads a grade file, the fan-in job publishes the check runs — and it is deliberately deferred out of this change. What bounds it meanwhile: `master` has no required status checks in either ruleset, so this is check-run forgery and signal suppression rather than a merge-gate bypass. Wiring up required checks is what makes that stop being true, and it should be sequenced after the split, not before.

**The client's dependencies are declared separately from the server's.** `client-test` has its own `Install client build deps` step rather than calling `install_deps.bash <distro>`, which is the *server's* list. Two reasons. The list is different in kind — the client needs no `rpm-build`, `openldap-devel`, `libzstd-devel`, `dpkg-dev` or gcc plugin headers — and on el9 the server's script ends in `build_gtest()`, whose cache probe cannot hit in a fresh `ubi9-minimal`, so every el9 leg cloned and compiled googletest from source for a library only `make run-tests` links. That put `github.com/google/googletest` on the critical path of three legs per PR, where an upstream outage reports as "client failed to build".

The list is the C client's own documented dependency set (its `README.md`, identical at `7.4.0` and at `stage`) plus the toolchain packages `ubi9-minimal` omits. It is still keyed by distro with no notion of a client version, so an older tag needing a package we no longer install, or a `stage` branch picking up a new one, shows up as a build error. That is why `make` and `make test` are separate steps: a build failure reports as a likely CI dependency gap and does *not* fail the job, a test failure reports as a server/client disagreement and does. "Failed to build" in the job summary is the trigger to extend the list — do that here rather than in `install_deps.bash`, whose signature `build-sign-deploy.yaml` also depends on.
